newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan says economy recovering despite stock plunge.
newsitem.headline: Japan says economy recovering despite stock plunge.

text.p: The Japanese government said on Tuesday it was sticking with its assessment that the economy is still growing despite fears in the financial markets that have sent share prices tumbling.

"Although stock prices are falling, the current state of the economy is that it is continuing to recover gradually and is more or less firm," an official of the government's Economic Planning Agency (EPA) told reporters.

The stock market seemed unimpressed by the soothing words however, resuming its month-long slide after a recovery on Monday. The benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares quickly dropped another 500 points in the first 30 minutes of trading and was down more than 400 points just before the close of the morning session.

The EPA's monthly assessment used the same phraseology to describe the country's economic conditions as in December and prescribed the same remedy to secure recovery. The report is closely watched by markets for signs of policy shifts.
"Our country's economy continues to recover, although the pace of the recovery is slow," the January report said.

"The government will continue to promote various economic structural reforms, including deregulation and will work towards managing the economy properly to strengthen economic recovery and secure the continuation of stable growth in the medium to longer term," the report said.

The EPA official said he felt that stocks were falling due to a long-term decline in Japanese corporations' profitability and excessive equity financing during the 1980s "bubble" of inflated asset prices.

Elements which had helped pushed up corporate profits -- weakness in the yen against the dollar, companies' restructuring efforts and low interest rates -- had been largely factored in, and sharp increases in company profits are unlikely, he said.
Market participants' grim economic outlook and uncertainties about the feasibility of various government reform plans had also fuelled the fall, he said.
The official said falls in share prices may have a negative impact on business sentiment, and thus corporate capital spending, but the impact was limited.
Corporate capital spending was on the rise and firms would be forced to carry out investment to survive various structural reforms in the economy, he said.
The report cited better employment data and growth in exports to back the government's optimism.
Although the unemployment rate was still near record-high levels, the number of unemployed people fell in November from a year earlier for the first time since April 1992.
The report said declines in domestic wholesale prices had stopped, mainly due to rise in global oil and copper prices and the yen's weakness against the dollar.
